mainTopic: Forced payment and תקנת הלל, then which properties and which cities count as בתי ערי חומה.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a debate about תקנת הלל. A seller of a house in a walled city may buy it back within a year, and הלל allowed him to pay even when the buyer hid from him. In two opposite versions, רבא learns from this whether money forced on someone counts as giving, for a גט given on condition of two hundred זוז. In each version, רב פפא pushes back on the proof. A new משנה then rules that everything inside a city wall is treated like בתי ערי חומה except fields, and the גמרא brings the פסוק sources for רבי יהודה and רבי מאיר. It then narrows their dispute to a quarry and a sand bed. רבי יוחנן shows that the argument over a house built into the wall comes from one פסוק about רחב. A second משנה defines a walled city: a real wall all around since the days of יהושע בן נון, and at least three courtyards of two houses each. The גמרא brings ברייתות that exclude roof-walls and טבריה, and that keep walled status for a city whose wall is gone. The amud ends by asking what a ברייתא means when it sorts the walled cities by region, and the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: רבא's inference: forced giving normally does not count
steps.stepSummary: Since הלל needed a special ordinance to make forced giving count, forced giving must normally not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: From the fact that הלל had to institute that giving against the receiver's will counts as giving, we see that normally, giving against someone's will does not count as giving.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind רבא's ruling in the first version. רבא learns a general rule from the fact that הלל needed to make an ordinance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If forced giving already counted, הלל would not have needed a special ordinance for the seller of a house. The fact that he needed one shows that the basic law is that forced giving is not giving. So a wife who forces the two hundred זוז on her husband has not fulfilled the condition of her גט.

keyTerms.meaning: to institute an ordinance (a rabbinic fix)
an act of giving or paying
in general, in an ordinary case

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not say that forced giving counts. It says the opposite: only because of הלל's special ordinance does it count for the house seller. Everywhere else, it does not.

phrases.english: From the fact that it was necessary for Hillel

phrases.aramaic: לְתַקּוֹנֵי נְתִינָה בְּעַל כׇּרְחוֹ הָוְיָא נְתִינָה,
phrases.english: to institute that giving against his will is considered giving,
phrases.notes: This is the house-seller ordinance: the money goes into the Temple chamber even though the buyer did not agree to take it.

phrases.english: this shows that in general

phrases.aramaic: נְתִינָה בְּעַל כׇּרְחוֹ לָא הָוְיָא נְתִינָה.
phrases.english: giving against his will is not considered giving.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning for רבא's ruling from the previous section, which says forced payment does not count.
steps.raayaObject: The general rule that giving against the receiver's will is not valid giving.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The need for תקנת הלל about the seller of a house in a walled city.
steps.whyThisMatters: This decides whether a conditional גט takes effect when the wife forces the money on her husband.

steps.title: Maybe הלל's ordinance was only needed when the buyer is absent
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא (or רב אשי) suggests that הלל's ordinance was needed only when the buyer is absent. Payment in person may count even against his will.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא objected, and some say it was רב אשי: But maybe הלל needed his ordinance only for paying when the buyer is not present. If the buyer is present, then whether he agrees or not, it counts as a valid gift.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא pushes back on רבא's proof. He offers another way to explain why הלל needed his ordinance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyers were hiding, so the money was being paid without them there. That alone could explain the ordinance. It does not have to mean that forced payment never counts. So we cannot prove from הלל that payment in the receiver's presence fails when he refuses.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa objects to this,
and some say it was Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: וְדִילְמָא כִּי אִיצְטְרִיכָא לֵיהּ לְהִלֵּל לְתַקּוֹנֵי
phrases.english: But perhaps when it was necessary for Hillel to institute
it was for paying not in his presence,
but in his presence,
whether with his consent or against his will,
it is a valid gift!
phrases.notes: Here 'gift' just means the money counts as properly handed over.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב פָּפָּא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב אָשֵׁי: וְדִילְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference in step 1 by offering another reason הלל needed his ordinance.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from הלל is rejected. רב פפא does not prove that forced giving counts. He shows that the proof does not hold.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ordinance may have been needed because the buyer was absent, not because forced giving fails.

steps.title: Second version: רבא rules that forced payment does count
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, רבא rules that the wife's payment of two hundred זוז counts even against her husband's will.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say the discussion went the opposite way. רבא said: From הלל's ordinance we learn that if a man says, "Here is your גט on condition that you give me two hundred זוז," and she gave it to him, then whether he agreed or not, it counts as giving.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives a second, opposite version of רבא's statement. Here רבא rules that forced payment is valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, רבא said forced giving does not count. In this version he says it does count, and the גט takes effect. He still learns this from תקנת הלל, but he reads the ordinance differently, as the next step explains.

keyTerms.meaning: Hillel's ordinance about redeeming houses in walled cities
two hundred zuz (a sum of money)

phrases.english: There are those who say: Rava says:
From the ordinance of Hillel we learn:
"This is your bill of divorce

phrases.aramaic: עַל מְנָת שֶׁתִּתְּנִי לִי מָאתַיִם זוּז״,
phrases.english: on condition that you give me two hundred zuz,"
and she gave it to him,
whether with his consent or against his will,
it is considered giving.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רָבָא: מִתַּקָּנָתוֹ שֶׁל הִלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opposite version of רבא's ruling from step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wife who pays the two hundred זוז has fulfilled the condition even if her husband refuses to take it, so the גט is valid.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two versions. In the first version, רבא says forced giving does not count. In this איכא דאמרי version, he says it does count.

steps.title: רבא's reason: הלל's ordinance was only for when the buyer is absent
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that הלל's ordinance was needed only when the buyer is absent. Payment in person counts even against the receiver's will.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is that הלל needed his ordinance only when the money is paid without the buyer present. If he is present, then whether he agrees or not, it counts as giving.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains why he reads הלל's ordinance as supporting forced payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא uses the same idea that רב פפא raised in the first version. The ordinance was only needed because the buyer was missing. When the payer hands the money to the receiver face to face, it counts even if he refuses. The wife pays her husband in his presence, so her payment works.

phrases.english: And when it was necessary for Hillel to institute his ordinance,
it was for paying not in his presence,
but in his presence,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין מִדַּעְתּוֹ בֵּין בְּעַל כׇּרְחוֹ הָוְיָא נְתִינָה.
phrases.english: whether with his consent or against his will, it is considered giving.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning for רבא's ruling in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Payment made in the receiver's presence is valid even against his will. הלל's ordinance was only for payment when the receiver is absent.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key line between paying in someone's presence and paying when he is absent.

steps.title: Maybe consent is always needed, and הלל only fixed the real problem
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא (or רב שימי בר אשי) suggests that consent may always be required, whether in person or not. הלל simply fixed the problem that came up in practice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא objected, and some say it was רב שימי בר אשי: But maybe, whether the buyer is present or not, giving with his consent counts and giving against his will does not. הלל just fixed the problem that actually needed fixing.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא pushes back on רבא's reasoning in the second version. He argues that הלל's ordinance does not show that payment in person works against the receiver's will.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The real problem in הלל's day was buyers hiding, so הלל made an ordinance for that case. That does not prove that a buyer who is present and refuses the money can be forced to accept it. Maybe forced giving never counts, in person or not, so רבא's proof falls away.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two versions of רבא. In the first, forced giving does not count, and רב פפא suggests payment in person might work. In the second, payment in person works, and רב פפא suggests consent might always be needed. In both versions, the objection rejects the proof from תקנת הלל.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa objects to this,
and some say it was Rav Shimi bar Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: וְדִילְמָא בֵּין בְּפָנָיו בֵּין שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו,
phrases.english: But perhaps, whether in his presence or not in his presence,
with his consent, yes, it counts;
against his will, no, it does not;
and Hillel instituted what was necessary!
phrases.notes: הלל only fixed the problem that was really happening, buyers hiding. He didn't cover a buyer who shows up and refuses.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב פָּפָּא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי: וְדִילְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבא's reasoning in step 4 by giving another explanation of why הלל made his ordinance.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from הלל in the second version is rejected. The objection does not decide the law.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ordinance may reflect the practical situation (hiding buyers), not a rule that payment in person works without consent.

steps.title: Everything inside the wall counts, except fields
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that anything inside a city wall is treated like בתי ערי חומה, except fields. רבי מאיר includes even the fields.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Anything inside the city wall is treated like houses in walled cities, except fields. רבי מאיר says: even fields.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It tells us which properties inside a walled city follow the special rules of בתי ערי חומה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A house in a walled city that was sold can only be bought back within one year. After that it belongs to the buyer forever and does not go back in יובל. The תנא קמא gives this status to everything inside the wall except fields, while רבי מאיר includes fields too.

keyTerms.meaning: Houses in walled cities, which have special rules for buying them back

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole sugya: how far the rule of בתי ערי חומה reaches beyond an ordinary house.

phrases.english: MISHNA
Anything that is inside the city wall
is like the houses of walled cities
except for the fields
Rabbi Meir says: Even the fields

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה after the earlier discussion of הלל's ordinance.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everything inside the wall has the status of בתי ערי חומה except fields. רבי מאיר includes fields too.

steps.title: A house built into the city wall
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says a house built into the wall is not like בתי ערי חומה. רבי שמעון says its outer wall counts as the city wall, so it is.
steps.simpleTranslation: A house built in the wall: רבי יהודה says it is not like the houses of walled cities. רבי שמעון says: its outer wall is its city wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a second dispute, about a house that is built right into the city wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that a house must be fully inside the wall to get this status, so a house that is part of the wall does not count. רבי שמעון says the house's outer side, which is the city wall itself, is enough to make it 'walled in.'

keyTerms.meaning: A house built into the city wall itself
The outer wall of the house

phrases.english: A house that is built in the wall

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ כְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: It is not like the houses of walled cities

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: כּוֹתֶל הַחִיצוֹן הִיא חוֹמָתוֹ
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says: The outer wall is its city wall

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second dispute in the same משנה about the edges of the category.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: a house built into the wall does not count. רבי שמעון: it counts, because its outer wall is the city wall.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's reading of the verse
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: 'אשר בעיר' includes other buildings and structures in the city, but the word 'בית' excludes fields. This is רבי יהודה's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The Rabbis taught: 'House': I only know a house. From where do we include olive-press houses, bathhouses, towers, dovecotes, pits, ditches and caves? The verse says 'that is in the city.' Maybe I should include even fields? The verse says 'house.' These are the words of רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that shows where the משנה's first rule comes from in the פסוק, following רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two words in the פסוק pull in opposite directions. 'אשר בעיר' widens the rule to anything in the city, and 'בית' narrows it so that fields, which are nothing like a house, are left out. That is why רבי יהודה is the תנא קמא of the משנה who excludes fields.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we learn to include?

phrases.english: GEMARA. The Rabbis taught
"House": I have only a house

phrases.aramaic: מִנַּיִן לְרַבּוֹת בָּתֵּי בַדִּים וּבָתֵּי מֶרְחֲצָאוֹת
phrases.english: From where do we include olive-press houses and bathhouses
and towers and dovecotes
and pits and ditches and caves?
The verse says: "That is in the city"
Might I include even the fields?
The verse says: "House"
These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בַּיִת — אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק source for the תנא קמא of the משנה, who is רבי יהודה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'אשר בעיר' includes all structures in the city, and 'בית' excludes fields.

steps.title: רבי מאיר includes even fields
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר reads 'אשר בעיר' as including everything in the city, even fields.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: It says 'house.' I only know a house. From where do we include olive-press houses, bathhouses, towers, dovecotes, pits, ditches, caves, and even fields? The verse says 'that is in the city.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with רבי מאיר's reading, which includes fields too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר uses the same words 'אשר בעיר' but lets them reach all the way to fields. He never says what the word 'בית' leaves out, and that gap sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: That is in the city (the words that widen the rule)

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: It says "house"
I have only a house

phrases.aramaic: מִנַּיִן לְרַבּוֹת בָּתֵּי בַדִּים וּבָתֵּי מֶרְחֲצָאוֹת
phrases.english: From where do we include olive-press houses and bathhouses
and towers and dovecotes
and pits, ditches and caves
and even fields?
The verse says: "That is in the city"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing reading, matching רבי מאיר in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'אשר בעיר' includes everything in the city, even fields.

steps.title: What does 'house' exclude for רבי מאיר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the פסוק says 'בית', so how can רבי מאיר include fields?
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written 'house'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי מאיר. The word 'בית' should be leaving something out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If everything, even fields, is included, then the word 'בית' seems to do nothing. For רבי יהודה it excluded fields. What does it exclude for רבי מאיר?

phrases.english: But it is written "house"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי מאיר's reading from step 9.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If fields are included, the word 'בית' has nothing left to exclude.

steps.title: The real dispute is a quarry and a sand bed
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא in the name of רב קטינא: everyone agrees 'בית' excludes fields. They argue about a quarry and a sand bed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רב קטינא: The difference between them is a quarry and a sand bed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by moving the dispute to a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now both תנאים agree that 'בית' excludes ordinary fields. The argument is only about a quarry and a sand bed, which are dug-out areas, a bit like a pit and a bit like a field. רבי מאיר treats them like houses, and רבי יהודה treats them like fields.

keyTerms.meaning: A sand bed or low hollow area

steps.confusionAlert: After this answer, רבי מאיר no longer includes ordinary fields. His 'even fields' is reread as meaning only a quarry and a sand bed.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said that Rav Ketina said
A quarry and a sand bed are the difference between them

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא: חוֹלְסִית וּמְצוּלָה אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the dispute to a borderline case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר includes every field, so 'בית' excludes nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'בית' excludes ordinary fields for everyone. The dispute is only over a quarry and a sand bed.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the answer
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא states openly that רבי מאיר treats a quarry and sand bed like houses, and רבי יהודה treats them like fields.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it was taught: A quarry and a sand bed: רבי מאיר says they are like houses. רבי יהודה says they are like fields.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up רב קטינא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא shows that רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה really did argue about these exact two places. That confirms the 'fields' in their dispute means a quarry and a sand bed.
steps.whatToRemember: Both תנאים agree that 'אשר בעיר' includes all buildings and structures in a walled city, and that 'בית' excludes ordinary fields. They argue only about a quarry and a sand bed: רבי מאיר says like houses, רבי יהודה says like fields.

phrases.english: And so it was taught: A quarry and a sand bed
Rabbi Meir says: Like houses
Rabbi Yehuda says: Like fields

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 11.
steps.raayaObject: רב קטינא's claim that the dispute is about a quarry and a sand bed
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recording רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה arguing over a quarry and a sand bed

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: a house built into the wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line in the משנה where רבי יהודה says a house built into the city wall is not treated like a house in a walled city.
steps.simpleTranslation: A house built right into the wall: רבי יהודה says it is not like the houses of walled cities.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה so it can explain it next. This step sets up רבי יוחנן's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is a house whose outer wall is the city wall itself. רבי יהודה says it does not get the special rules of בתי ערי חומה, and the משנה brings רבי שמעון, who disagrees. The quote opens a new topic after the ברייתא about the quarry and sand bed.

keyTerms.meaning: A house built into the city wall itself
Houses in cities that are surrounded by a wall, which have special sale and redemption rules

phrases.english: A house that is built in the wall,
Rabbi Yehuda says:
it is not like the houses of walled cities.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּיִת הַבָּנוּי בַּחוֹמָה, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of quarries and sand beds and turns to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, a house built into the city wall does not have the status of a house in a walled city.

steps.title: Both sides learn from the same verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון both base their views on one פסוק, the one describing רחב's house in the wall of יריחו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Both of them learned from the same verse: "Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was in the side of the wall, and she lived on the wall."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן finds the source for the argument. He says both תנאים are reading the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sides do not have two different sources. They read one פסוק in two ways, and the key words are "וּבַחוֹמָה הִיא יוֹשָׁבֶת". The next step shows how each side reads it.

keyTerms.meaning: A verse from the Torah or the Prophets
They expounded, meaning they learned a law from the verse

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
And both of them expounded one verse,
phrases.notes: "Both of them" means רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון from the משנה.

phrases.english: "Then she let them down by a cord through the window,
for her house was in the side of the wall,
and on the wall she dwelt."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind the argument quoted in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both views about a house in the wall come from the same פסוק in יהושע.

steps.title: How each side reads the verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון reads the פסוק simply, so a house in the wall counts as part of the walled city. רבי יהודה reads "she lived on the wall" to mean she lived in the wall and not in the walled city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון follows the simple meaning of the verse. רבי יהודה holds that "she lived on the wall" means she lived in the wall, not in the walled city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how each תנא reads the same words of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי שמעון, the פסוק just describes where her house was. A house attached to the wall is part of the walled city. רבי יהודה reads "בַּחוֹמָה" as a separate place: someone living in the wall is not living in the walled city, so the house does not count as one of the בתי ערי חומה.

keyTerms.meaning: The simple, plain meaning of the verse

steps.whatToRemember: Same פסוק, two readings: רבי שמעון says a house in the wall is part of the walled city, and רבי יהודה says it belongs to the wall and not to the city.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon holds
according to the simple meaning of the verse,
and Rabbi Yehuda holds:
"On the wall she dwelt"
and not in the walled city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the two readings of the פסוק quoted in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שמעון: a house in the wall counts as part of the walled city. רבי יהודה: it counts as being in the wall, not in the city.

steps.title: משנה: cities that do not count as walled
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that two kinds of cities are not treated as walled: a city whose only wall is its rooftops, and a city that was not walled from the time of יהושע בן נון.
steps.simpleTranslation: A city whose rooftops are its wall, or a city that has not been surrounded by a wall since the days of יהושע בן נון, is not like the houses of walled cities.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists cities that do not get the status of a walled city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two conditions are added here. The wall has to be a real wall, not a row of joined rooftops. The wall also has to date back to when יהושע בן נון entered the land, so a wall built later is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה, the opening text the גמרא discusses
Its rooftops are its wall, meaning there is no real wall, only joined houses
From the days of יהושע בן נון, when the land was first conquered

steps.confusionAlert: A city with a wall today is not automatically a walled city for this law. The wall must go back to the time of יהושע בן נון.

phrases.english: MISHNA
A city whose rooftops are its wall,
and one that is not surrounded by a wall
from the days of Yehoshua bin Nun,
is not like the houses of walled cities.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה that defines which cities count as walled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city walled only by its rooftops, or not walled since the time of יהושע, does not have walled-city status.

steps.title: משנה: what a real walled city is, with examples
steps.stepSummary: The משנה defines a walled city: at least three courtyards with two houses each, surrounded by a wall since the time of יהושע. It then lists examples, including ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the houses of walled cities: a place with three courtyards of two houses each, surrounded by a wall since the days of יהושע בן נון. Examples are the old fort of ציפורי, the fortress of גוש חלב, old יודפת, גמלא, גדוד, חדיד, אונו, ירושלים, and other places like them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now gives the positive definition of a walled city and names real places as examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two requirements: a minimum size of three courtyards with two houses in each, and a wall dating from the time of יהושע. The list is only a set of examples, since the משנה ends with "and others like them."

keyTerms.meaning: Courtyards, each shared by a group of houses
Others similar to them, showing the list is only examples

steps.whatToRemember: A walled city needs at least three courtyards of two houses each and a wall from the time of יהושע בן נון.

phrases.english: And these are the houses of walled cities:
three courtyards of two houses,
phrases.notes: He means at least three courtyards, with two houses in each one.

phrases.aramaic: מוּקֶּפֶת חוֹמָה מִימוֹת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן,
phrases.english: surrounded by a wall from the days of Yehoshua bin Nun,
such as the old fort of Tzippori,
and the fortress of Gush Chalav,
and old Yodfat, and Gamla,
and Gedod, and Chadid, and Ono, and Jerusalem,
and likewise others similar to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After saying what does not count, the משנה says what does count.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A walled city has at least three courtyards of two houses each and a wall from the time of יהושע. Examples are listed, including ירושלים.

steps.title: ברייתא: no roof-walls, and טבריה is excluded
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the word "חומה" that a wall made of rooftops does not count. From "סביב" (around) it learns that טבריה is excluded, because the sea serves as its wall on one side.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: "Wall" means a real wall, not a wall of roofs. "Around" excludes טבריה, whose sea is its wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives a פסוק source for the משנה's rule about roof-walls and adds another case, טבריה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "חומה" requires an actual wall, which is the source for the משנה's rooftop rule. The word "סביב" requires a wall all the way around. So a city where water forms one side, like טבריה, does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: A wall made of roofs, the joined rooftops of houses
Around, meaning a wall that fully surrounds the city
To exclude, coming to leave out a certain case

phrases.english: GEMARA
The Rabbis taught:
"Wall" — and not a wall of roofs,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:30. This matches the משנה's case of a city whose rooftops are its wall.

phrases.english: "Around" — excluding Tiberias,
whose sea is its wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק source for the משנה's rule about rooftops and adds the case of טבריה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a real wall that fully surrounds the city counts. Roof-walls do not count, and a city with water on one side, like טבריה, is excluded.

steps.title: A wall that existed in the past still counts
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בר יוסי learns from the spelling "לוא" that a city which had a wall before keeps its walled status even without a wall now.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בר יוסי says: "Which has a wall" teaches that even if it has no wall now, it counts if it had one before.
steps.whatsHappening: Another תנא adds a rule based on how a word in the פסוק is spelled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "לוא" (has) is written with an א, so it can also be read as "לא" (does not have). Reading both ways together teaches that a city which has no wall now but had one before is still a walled city. This fits with the משנה's focus on a wall from the time of יהושע.

keyTerms.meaning: Written with an א, so it can mean "has" or "does not have"

steps.whyThisMatters: The status of a walled city depends on its history, not only on how it looks today.
steps.whatToRemember: A city that had a wall in the past keeps its walled-city status even after the wall is gone.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer bar Yosei says:
"Which has a wall" —
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:30. "לוא" is spelled with an א, so it could also be read "which has no wall."

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ עַכְשָׁיו
phrases.english: even though it does not have one now
but it had one before.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בַּר יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: ״אֲשֶׁר לוֹא חוֹמָה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another lesson about walls from the same פסוק, this time about a wall that no longer stands.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city that had a wall in the past keeps its walled status even if it has no wall now.

steps.title: A ברייתא tells us where the walled cities from the משנה are located
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's opening words about walled cities. Then it brings a ברייתא that places גמלא in the גליל, גדוד in עבר הירדן, and חדיד, אונו and ירושלים in יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And these are the houses of walled cities, etc.' A ברייתא taught: גמלא is in the גליל, גדוד is across the Jordan, and חדיד, אונו and ירושלים are in יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה's list of walled cities from step 17. It brings a ברייתא that tells us which region each of those cities is in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only gave a list of city names. The ברייתא adds new information: it sorts those cities into three regions of ארץ ישראל. It is not yet clear why the ברייתא bothers to do this, and the next step asks exactly that.

keyTerms.meaning: Walled cities, which have special rules for selling houses
The Galilee, the northern region of ארץ ישראל
The land on the east side of the Jordan River
Judea, the southern region around ירושלים

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵלּוּ הֵן בָּתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: And these are the houses of walled cities, etc.
phrases.notes: These are the opening words of the משנה's list from step 17. The 'etc.' means the rest of that list.

phrases.english: It was taught: Gamla is in the Galilee,
and Gedod is across the Jordan,
and Hadid and Ono and Jerusalem are in Judea.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵלּוּ הֵן בָּתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה כּוּ׳. תָּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה's list of walled cities from step 17, after the discussion of the פסוקים in steps 18-19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא sorts the walled cities into regions: גמלא in the גליל, גדוד in עבר הירדן, and חדיד, אונו and ירושלים in יהודה.

steps.title: What is the ברייתא trying to say?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא means by listing these cities by region. Is it saying these are the only walled cities there?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it saying?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא's point is. This is a setup question, and the answer comes in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Listing only a few cities per region could make it sound like these are the only walled cities in each region. That reading is hard to accept, since the משנה itself said there are other similar cities. So the גמרא asks what the ברייתא really means.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is he saying?' The גמרא asks for the meaning or purpose of a statement

steps.confusionAlert: This question is not an attack. The גמרא is not saying the ברייתא is wrong. It only wants to understand what the ברייתא is telling us.

phrases.english: What is it saying?
phrases.notes: He means: why list these few cities by region? Surely there were other walled cities in these areas too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the meaning of the ברייתא quoted in step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the ברייתא means by naming these cities by region, since it seems unlikely they are the only walled cities in those areas.
